new.title: Walk the 129 metre colonnade of the Kurhaus
new.desc: The Kurhaus is Wiesbaden's grand spa house, opened in 1907 to a design by Friedrich von Thiersch after the older 1810 building was torn down. Its colonnade is 129 metres long and is billed as the longest columned hall in Europe, and a lawn with two cascade fountains, the Bowling Green, sits in front of the entrance.
new.tip: Wander through the colonnade first, then settle on a bench on the Bowling Green and look back at the portico. It is at its best in the evening light.

new.title: Stroll the English landscape Kurpark
new.desc: The Kurpark was laid out in 1852 as an English landscape garden on 75,000 square metres in the Rambach valley. A pond with a fountain shooting about six metres high is its centrepiece, two sandstone columns from the old 1810 Kurhaus stand at the Nizzaplätzchen, and a bust of Dostoevsky hides among the trees.
new.tip: Start behind the Kurhaus and keep walking up the valley towards Sonnenberg, where the city park turns into woodland.

new.title: Look up at the 88 metre red brick Marktkirche
new.desc: The neo-Gothic Marktkirche was built between 1853 and 1862 by Carl Boos and was the first pure brick building in the Duchy of Nassau. Its west tower rises about 88 metres and is still the tallest building in the city, and its organ, expanded to 85 stops, is the largest in its church district.
new.tip: Step inside to see the nave, then cross the Schlossplatz for the best angle on the tower. If an organ concert is on, plan around it.

new.title: Find the golden lion on Schlossplatz by the Stadtschloss
new.desc: The classicist Stadtschloss was built from 1837 to 1841 for the Duke of Nassau and later became a spring residence of Kaiser Wilhelm II. Since the state of Hesse was founded in 1946 it has housed the Hessian parliament, and its domed central hall holds a chandelier with 24,000 pieces of Bohemian crystal. On the square outside stands the 1753 Marktbrunnen, topped by a golden Nassau lion.
new.tip: The parliament can be visited on guided tours, so check what is offered before you go. The square itself is free any time and sits beside the old town hall of 1610.

new.title: Step up to the golden domes of the Russian church
new.desc: High on the Neroberg, the Russian Orthodox church of St Elisabeth was built from 1847 to 1855 by Duke Adolf of Nassau as a burial church for his young wife, Grand Duchess Elisabeth Mikhailovna, who died in childbirth. Five gilded onion domes crown it, and one of the largest Russian Orthodox cemeteries in Western Europe lies in the forest nearby.
new.tip: Ride the Nerobergbahn up, or walk through the Nerotal park, and keep your voice low inside. The cemetery can be viewed on request at the church.

new.title: Admire the Rhine-side baroque of Schloss Biebrich
new.desc: Friedrich Joachim Stengel began this baroque three-wing palace in 1734 for the princes of Nassau-Usingen, who made Biebrich their residence in 1744. Its central rotunda holds a festival hall with a dome modelled on the Pantheon in Rome, and the whole front faces the Rhine.
new.tip: Walk along the river meadow in front of it for the full sweep of the facade, then continue into the park behind. There is a cafe on the ground floor of the rotunda.

new.title: Wander the long park behind Schloss Biebrich
new.desc: The palace park stretches about 1,200 metres north from the castle and is 300 metres wide, with the Mosbach stream running through it. It began as a French formal garden on an artificial plateau and was later turned into a landscape park, and it is freely accessible.
new.tip: Walk it from the palace to the far end and back, and bring a picnic for the lawns.

new.title: Touch the Roman Heidenmauer, the city's oldest wall
new.desc: The Heidenmauer is the best-known Roman monument in Wiesbaden, which was called Aquae Mattiacorum in antiquity. Traditionally dated to around 370 AD, it stands up to 10 metres high with a base about 2.3 metres thick, and roughly 80 metres of it are visible today. The little Römertor gate beside it was added in 1903.
new.tip: It sits on the edge of the old town, so combine it with a walk to the Marktplatz. The gate's viewing platform is reached only on guided tours.

new.title: Promenade down Wilhelmstraße, the grand boulevard
new.desc: Wilhelmstraße was laid out in 1810 by city master builder Christian Zais and named after Duke Wilhelm of Nassau. Only one side is lined with trees, and along its length stand the Kurhaus, the state theatre, the classicist Erbprinzenpalais and the Villa Clementine, with the Warmer Damm park on the east side.
new.tip: Walk it from the Kurhaus end south to the Rheinstraße, ideally in the afternoon when the cafes open their terraces.

new.title: Peek into the Villa Clementine literature house
new.desc: This historicist villa was built from 1878 to 1882 for the Mainz businessman Ernst Meyer, who bought the plot for his wife Clementine, who died shortly before it was finished. It now serves as a Literaturhaus with readings and events and is the seat of the Wiesbaden press club, with a cafe on the upper floor.
new.tip: Check the event programme, since an evening reading in the villa is the best way to see the interior. Combine it with the Wilhelmstraße walk.

new.title: See the twin towers of the Ringkirche
new.desc: Johannes Otzen built this neo-Romanesque church from 1892 to 1894 as the first Protestant church in Germany to follow the Wiesbaden Programme, with altar, pulpit and organ stacked centrally and the pews in a semicircle so everyone sees the preacher. Its 65 metre twin tower closes the sight line at the end of the Rheinstraße.
new.tip: Stand at the far end of Rheinstraße for the full axis, then go inside for the concert-hall feel of the nave.

new.title: Find Art Nouveau steel and stained glass at the Lutherkirche
new.desc: Built from 1908 to 1910 to a design by Friedrich Pützer, the Lutherkirche is a Jugendstil church with a 50 metre tower and an elliptical interior under a rib vault that seats 1,200. Otto Linnemann created its stained glass and painted decoration in 1911, and a 1911 Walcker organ is still played.
new.tip: Visit when the church is open or attend a concert, since the acoustics are the reason people come.

new.title: Marvel at the neo-Gothic Bonifatiuskirche on Luisenplatz
new.desc: St Boniface, built from 1844 to 1849, is the main Catholic church of Wiesbaden, a neo-Gothic hall church whose two 68 metre towers dominate the classicist Luisenplatz. It is a good counterpart to the red brick Marktkirche a few minutes away.
new.tip: Go in for the quiet after the busy Luisenplatz, then walk up Friedrichstraße to the old town.

new.title: Stroll the Bergkirchenviertel and see its Gothic Revival church
new.desc: The Bergkirche was completed in 1879 in Gothic Revival to a design by Johannes Otzen, built to bring the altar and pulpit close to the congregation. It crowns a lively quarter of small shops, wine bars and cafes around Obere Webergasse and Mauergasse, and also serves as a concert venue.
new.tip: Make it your wine-bar crawl base: start at the church, then wander down Obere Webergasse and Mauergasse.

new.title: Read the Schiller motto on the Hessian State Theatre
new.desc: The neobaroque Staatstheater was built from 1892 to 1894 by the Viennese firm Fellner and Helmer, funded by Kaiser Wilhelm II, who opened it in 1894. Its gable carries a quote from Schiller about the dignity of humankind, the foyer staircase has a red canopy with the Prussian eagle, and the Großes Haus seats 1,041.
new.tip: Catch a performance if you can; the International May Festival of theatre and music fills the building every May. Otherwise the colonnade out front is free to enjoy.

new.title: Climb to the Monopteros on the Neroberg
new.desc: At 245 metres, the Neroberg is Wiesbaden's own hill, rising about 130 metres above the Schlossplatz. Its Monopteros, a temple-like viewpoint designed by Philipp Hoffmann, gives a wide view over the city, and the hillside vineyard of 4.1 hectares grows only Riesling.
new.tip: Walk up through the Nerotal park or ride the Nerobergbahn, and pause at the vineyard on your way to the viewpoint. Sunset is best.

new.title: Meet Jawlensky and Fluxus at Museum Wiesbaden
new.desc: Museum Wiesbaden is one of five Hessian state museums, a two-in-one house of art and natural history founded in 1825. It holds 57 paintings and 35 graphic works by Alexej von Jawlensky, the largest collection of his work outside the Norton Simon Museum, a Jugendstil collection, and works by Beuys and Nam June Paik. The first Fluxus festival took place here in 1962.
new.tip: Allow two hours and do not skip the natural history floors, which hold about a million objects. A good rainy-day anchor.

new.title: Walk into the white granite Museum Reinhard Ernst
new.desc: Opened on 23 June 2024 at Wilhelmstraße 1, this museum is devoted to abstract art, showing works from the private collection of the entrepreneur Reinhard Ernst, which holds more than 960 pieces. The building by Japanese architect Fumihiko Maki is clad in white granite and wraps around a glass-roofed atrium, with column-free exhibition rooms.
new.tip: Look at the atrium before the galleries, since the architecture is half of the visit. Pair it with a Wilhelmstraße stroll.

new.title: Ride the water-powered Nerobergbahn up the hill
new.desc: The Nerobergbahn opened on 25 September 1888 and still runs on water ballast: the car at the top is filled with up to 7,000 litres of water, and its weight pulls the other car uphill. The 438 metre track climbs 83 metres, and it is the last funicular of this type in Germany.
new.tip: It runs from Good Friday to the end of October. Ride up for the view and the vineyard, then walk back down through the Nerotal park.

new.title: Soak in the Art Nouveau Kaiser-Friedrich-Therme
new.desc: Built from 1910 to 1913 by August O. Pauly, this Reform-architecture and Jugendstil bath is fed by the Adlerquelle, the city's second-largest thermal spring after the Kochbrunnen, with water at about 64.6 degrees. Its Irish-Roman bath has mosaic tiles restored in 1999, and the sauna area covers 1,450 square metres.
new.tip: Go for the Irish-Roman circuit and plan at least two relaxed hours; book ahead for busy weekends.

new.title: Try your luck at the Wiesbaden casino
new.desc: Gambling in Wiesbaden goes back to a privilege granted in 1771, and Dostoevsky won 10,400 francs here in 1863 before losing his travel money and writing The Gambler in 26 days in 1866. Today roulette, blackjack and poker are played in the former Weinsaal of the Kurhaus, with slot machines in the colonnade.
new.tip: Check the entry rules on the casino website before going, and set a limit before you walk in.

new.title: Swim above the city at the Opelbad
new.desc: Funded by Wilhelm von Opel's foundation, the Opelbad opened in June 1934 on the south slope of the Neroberg, about 80 metres above the city centre. The New Building style pool is kept at a constant 24 degrees by solar technology, and its panoramic terrace restaurant is open to all visitors.
new.tip: Go on a warm day for a swim with a view, or just visit the restaurant terrace for the panorama.

new.title: Climb the keep of Burg Sonnenberg
new.desc: Counts Heinrich II and Ruprecht of Nassau began this hilltop castle in 1200 to guard Wiesbaden against the rival Eppstein family, and the keep was finished in 1208. After a restoration from 2005 to 2015 the ruin is accessible again, with a covered viewing platform in the keep.
new.tip: Follow the Kurpark valley up from the city, about an hour on foot, and check opening times before climbing the keep.

new.title: Walk the English Nerotal park below the Neroberg
new.desc: The Nerotalanlagen are a roughly one kilometre long, 5.7 hectare park laid out in the English landscape style in 1897 and 1898, now under heritage protection. The Nerobergbahn viaduct of 1888 bounds it to the north, and the old Kurhaus Bad Nerotal of 1907 now houses the thalhaus theatre.
new.tip: A gentle walk that ends at the funicular station; combine it with a ride up and a descent on foot.

new.title: Order breakfast at the Viennese Café Maldaner
new.desc: Adam Maldaner started a bakery in Friedrichstraße in 1859, and in 1908 his son built the present Maldaner house on Marktstraße 34. A pastry shop and café opened there in 1923, and in 2011 it became the first café in Germany to receive the Original Viennese Coffee House award.
new.tip: Reserve ahead for breakfast, especially on weekends, and combine it with a stroll through the weekly market nearby.

new.title: Sip Rheingau Riesling at Balthasar Ress on Mauergasse
new.desc: Balthasar Ress began as the Gasthof Ress in Hattenheim in 1870 and is now a wine estate in the Rheingau. Its Weinbar and Vinothek on Mauergasse is one of the cosy wine bars on the street that Wiesbaden people head to after the weekly market.
new.tip: Order a glass of Rheingau Riesling, and walk on to the other bars on the same street.
new.q: Balthasar Ress Weinbar Vinothek, Mauergasse 10, Wiesbaden

new.title: Have an aperitif at Wine in the Hood
new.desc: Wine in the Hood is a wine bar on Obere Webergasse in the Bergkirchenviertel, a street where people gather outside in summer. The city tourist office recommends it, together with its neighbour Weinod, for an aperitif or a glass of wine.
new.tip: Arrive in the early evening and take a seat outside, then wander to the other bars on the street.
new.q: Wine in the Hood, Obere Webergasse 49, Wiesbaden

new.title: Drink Neroberg Riesling with a view at Chateau Nero
new.desc: Chateau Nero is a seasonal wine stand on a plateau above the Neroberg vineyard, with a panorama over Wiesbaden. The vineyard is worked by Kloster Eberbach, and the stand serves Rheingau wines including the Neroberger Riesling grown on the slope, plus small food items.
new.tip: It opens on longer hours in summer and shorter ones in winter, with Mondays closed in winter, so check the calendar. Take the Nerobergbahn up and walk the last stretch.

new.title: Eat Handkäs mit Musik at the Schoppenhof
new.desc: The Schoppenhof is a traditional Apfelwein pub in the Westend, opened in early 2017 in the former Weisenburger Hof. It serves hearty Hessian classics such as Handkäs mit Musik, Frankfurt green sauce with potatoes and eggs, and schnitzel, with a house Speierling cider and a cloudy Haus Schoppen from the Stier cider press in Maintal.
new.tip: Reserve by phone, since the room is small, and try the Speierling cider if you like it tart and tannic.

new.title: Order a hearty cutlet at Zum Kortheuer on Nerostraße
new.desc: Zum Kortheuer is a long-running German restaurant on Nerostraße, which was cut through the old town wall near the Kochbrunnen in 1809. The city tourist office lists it for rustic German dishes such as pork chops and potato soup, and the street itself is known for small shops, cafés and restaurants.
new.tip: Take an outside table on Nerostraße and order the house classics, then stroll on to the Kochbrunnen.

new.title: Brunch in the Old Courthouse at Delikt Tagbar
new.desc: Delikt Tagbar sits in the historic Alter Gerichtsbau and serves breakfast with ingredients from local producers, including coffee from the Maldaner roastery. Sunday is brunch day, in the setting of the old courthouse.
new.tip: Book a table for Sunday brunch and take your time in the high rooms.
new.q: Delikt Tagbar im Alten Gericht, Gerichtstraße 2, Wiesbaden

new.title: Eat gelato on the steps facing the State Theatre
new.desc: Mazzucco is an ice cream parlour in the colonnades by the Hessisches Staatstheater, and the classic way to enjoy it is on the steps in front, looking across to the theatre. The Warmer Damm park lies right behind.
new.tip: Take your cone to the Warmer Damm and sit by the pond on a warm afternoon.

new.title: Pick up a bag of beans at Maldaner Coffee Roasters
new.desc: Maldaner Coffee Roasters on Mauergasse is known for very good coffee, and local cafés such as Delikt Tagbar use its beans. It is a friendly stop on the wine and coffee street of the Bergkirchenviertel.
new.tip: Have a coffee at the counter and buy a bag for home, then continue to the wine bars nearby.

new.title: Visit the Henkell sparkling wine castle in Biebrich
new.desc: Adam Henkell founded his wine firm in Mainz in 1832, and Otto Henkell created the Henkell Trocken brand in 1894. The cellar building, which the firm moved into in 1909, was designed by Paul Bonatz in a neoclassical style on Biebricher Allee, and locals call it Schloss Henkell.
new.tip: Guided cellar tours with a sparkling wine tasting have been offered, but booking is needed, so check with Henkell first. Schloss Biebrich is a short ride away.

new.title: Taste the 66 degree thermal water at the Kochbrunnen
new.desc: The Kochbrunnen is the best-known hot spring in Wiesbaden, a sodium chloride spring first mentioned in 1366 and now flowing at about 66 degrees. It yields roughly 360 litres a minute, tastes strongly salty, and smells faintly of sulphur.
new.tip: Bring a cup, take a sip and see how long you can stand it, then reward yourself with a coffee in Nerostraße.

new.title: Climb the tower of the Kurfürstliche Burg in Eltville
new.desc: Archbishop Balduin began building this riverside castle in 1330, and it was completed in 1345 after an older tower castle was destroyed in 1301. A 24 metre fortified tower holds a Gutenberg memorial and a printing museum, and more than 118 steps lead up to a lookout over the Rhine, while a 40 step spiral staircase leads down to the dungeon.
new.tip: Climb to the Wehrplatte for the view, then wander the town known as the rose town. The tourist information is on the ground floor.
new.q: Kurfürstliche Burg, Burgstraße, Eltville am Rhein

new.title: Walk the Cistercian cloisters of Kloster Eberbach
new.desc: Monks sent from Clairvaux founded this abbey on 13 February 1136, and it became one of the most significant Romanesque and early Gothic sites in Hesse. A great cask first filled in 1500 held about 71,000 litres, and the abbey shipped its wine to Cologne each year on boats called Eberbacher Bock. Interior scenes of the film The Name of the Rose were shot here in the winter of 1985 and 1986.
new.tip: Allow half a day, and walk the surrounding vineyards if the weather is kind.

new.title: Meet Germania at the Niederwald monument
new.desc: The Niederwalddenkmal above Rüdesheim was built from 1877 to 1883 to commemorate German unification and was inaugurated on 28 September 1883. The monument is 38.18 metres high, and the Germania statue on top is 12.5 metres tall, holding a laurel crown in her right hand and a lowered sword in her left. It overlooks the Rhine valley and the town of Bingen.
new.tip: Take the cable car up and walk back down along the vineyards, or follow the path from the monument to the viewpoints.

new.title: Hear the Gregorian chant in Kiedrich's Gothic church
new.desc: The Gothic church of St Valentinus in Kiedrich was completed in 1493 and is nicknamed a treasure chest of Gothic art. Its organ, from around 1500 with about 960 pipes, is described as the oldest playable church organ in Germany, and the Kiedricher Chorbuben have sung Latin Gregorian chant here since 1333.
new.tip: Time your visit for a service or concert to hear the choir, and wander the wine village afterwards.

new.title: Find the keep of Burg Scharfenstein above Kiedrich
new.desc: Construction of this castle began around 1160 as part of the border fortifications of the Archbishopric of Mainz and was largely finished by 1260. It has been a ruin since the 16th century, and the surviving keep, visible from afar, appears in the municipal seal of Kiedrich.
new.tip: Walk up from Kiedrich through the vineyards for the view over the Rheingau.

new.title: Spot the shield wall of Burg Ehrenfels from the Rhine path
new.desc: This castle ruin stands halfway between Rüdesheim and Assmannshausen on the steep slope of the Rüdesheimer Berg, one of the best vineyard sites in Germany. Of the old toll castle the 4.6 metre thick, 20 metre high shield wall survives with two 33 metre corner towers, and it is part of the UNESCO Upper Middle Rhine Valley since 2002.
new.tip: Because of breeding peregrine falcons it can be viewed only from the outside, so enjoy it from the riverside path.

new.title: Raise a glass to Queen Victoria at the Hochheim monument
new.desc: Queen Victoria and Prince Albert visited Hochheim in 1845, and the town's wine became known in England as Hock. A neo-Gothic monument in the vineyard honours the visit, and the vineyard was named Königin-Victoriaberg after it.
new.tip: Walk the vineyards around the monument and finish with a glass of Hochheim Riesling in town.

new.title: Climb to the Hexenturm, Idstein's 42 metre witch tower
new.desc: The Hexenturm is the oldest building in Idstein, the keep of the old castle, and about 42 metres tall. The old town below it is full of half-timbered houses, mostly from the 16th and 17th centuries, and the oldest surviving residential house dates from 1410.
new.tip: Pair the tower with a walk through the Fachwerk lanes of the old town.

new.title: Look at the Rubens-school ceiling of the Unionskirche in Idstein
new.desc: The Unionskirche began as a collegiate church with roots in the 13th century and was rebuilt in the Gothic style in the mid-14th century. In the 17th century its nave ceiling was covered with large oil paintings from the school of Rubens.
new.tip: Go in during opening hours and look straight up.

new.title: Admire the Killinger-Haus, Idstein's showpiece of timber
new.desc: The Killingerhaus was built in 1615 at the edge of König-Adolf-Platz towards the Unionskirche. It has served as a museum and tourist office since 1987, in a town on the German Timber-Frame Road.
new.tip: Stop by the tourist office, then stroll the old town; the Renaissance Schloss above is open on guided tours.

new.title: Cross the moat of Burg Stahleck above Bacharach
new.desc: Burg Stahleck was built on a crag about 160 metres up, probably around the 12th century, with a water-filled moat that is a rarity in Germany. Destroyed in the late 17th century and rebuilt in the 20th, it now serves as a youth hostel with a commanding view of the Rhine gorge towards the Lorelei.
new.tip: Climb the steep path from the town and carry on to the ruin of the Wernerkapelle on the way.

new.title: Glide over the vineyards on the Rüdesheim cable car
new.desc: The Seilbahn Rüdesheim opened in 1954, runs about 1,400 metres and climbs 209 metres to the Niederwald monument. It replaced an earlier cog railway, and you float directly above the vineyards.
new.tip: Ride up one way and walk down through the vines, or take both legs for the views.
new.q: Rüdesheimer Seilbahn, Oberstraße 37, Rüdesheim am Rhein

new.title: Hear a century of orchestrions at Siegfried's music cabinet
new.desc: Siegfried's Mechanisches Musikkabinett in the 15th-century Brömserhof directly above Drosselgasse holds over 400 self-playing instruments, from tiny music boxes to a giant orchestrion, with a 22 bell Meissen porcelain glockenspiel on show. Visits are guided and include live demonstrations of some pieces.
new.tip: Reserve ahead via the official site, and make it your rainy-day plan in Rüdesheim.
new.q: Siegfrieds Mechanisches Musikkabinett, Oberstraße 29, Rüdesheim am Rhein

new.title: Watch the wolves and bears at the Fasanerie wildlife park
new.desc: This 23 hectare animal and plant park in the Wiesbaden city forest opened on 31 March 1955, though its roots go back to a pheasant breeding established around 1750. About 250 animals of roughly 50 species live here, with brown bears and wolves in a large enclosure, and the baroque hunting lodge by Friedrich Joachim Stengel, built from 1744 to 1749, houses a restaurant.
new.tip: Check the admission policy before you go, and bring the children for the walk through the forest.

new.title: Squeeze down Drosselgasse, Rüdesheim's wine lane
new.desc: The Drosselgasse is a cobbled lane only 2 metres wide and about 144 metres long, lined with wine houses and visited by about three million people a year. First mentioned in the 15th century as a quarter for Rhine boatmen, most of its houses were destroyed in an air raid on 25 November 1944, and much was rebuilt in the 1950s.
new.tip: Go midweek or in the early evening to avoid the worst crowds, and sit in a wine house for a glass of Rheingau Riesling.

new.title: Taste red Spätburgunder from the Assmannshausen Höllenberg
new.desc: Assmannshausen is famed for its red wine, Pinot noir called Spätburgunder, that resembles red Burgundy. The Kloster Eberbach domain here dates its red wine tradition to the founding years of the abbey, and the Höllenberg slope with its purple slate soil gives the wine a pithy character.
new.tip: Book a tasting at the estate, and pair it with a walk along the Rhine to the Burg Ehrenfels ruin.

new.title: Drink Riesling where Spätlese was born at Schloss Johannisberg
new.desc: The 50 hectare vineyard of Schloss Johannisberg is planted exclusively with Riesling, and the story goes that in 1775 a courier arrived late with the harvest request, giving noble rot a chance and creating the first Spätlese. Metternich took over the estate in 1816, and a 260 metre vaulted cellar finished in 1721 holds bottles as old as 1748.
new.tip: The castle is closed to the public, but the terrace wine bar is open, so enjoy a glass on the terrace.

new.title: Dine by the moated tower of Schloss Vollrads
new.desc: The oldest wine record of Schloss Vollrads dates from 1211, and its moated residential tower, reached only by a bridge, goes back to the 14th century, with an octagonal stair tower added in 1471. The estate has a restaurant in the Kavaliershaus with an Orangerie, and a seasonal wine tavern in the courtyard.
new.tip: Most of the castle is closed except during events, so enjoy it from the courtyard tavern.

new.title: Taste Lorch wines in the Renaissance Hilchenhaus
new.desc: The Hilchenhaus in Lorch was built from 1546 to 1548 for Field Marshal Johann Hilchen von Lorch and is called the most beautiful Renaissance building on the Middle Rhine. The ground floor holds the Hilchenkeller restaurant, and the second floor has a Vinothek and the tourist information.
new.tip: Pop into the Vinothek for a Lorch Riesling, and walk the Rhine path afterwards.

new.title: Find a Straußwirtschaft in Eltville's old town
new.desc: A Straußwirtschaft is a seasonal tavern run by winemakers who pour their own wines directly, often with small plates to match. Weinbau Folch at Holzstraße 4 is a small winery in the centre of Eltville with about 4 hectares of vineyards between Rauenthal and Assmannshausen, and runs open tavern dates through the season.
new.tip: Check the dates before heading out, since a Straußwirtschaft is open only on certain days.
new.q: Weinbau Folch, Holzstraße 4, Eltville am Rhein
